content: In physical chemistry, saturation refers to the point at which a solution can no longer dissolve additional amounts of a substance. When this point is reached, any extra substance added will form a precipitate. This maximum concentration, known as the saturation point, is influenced by the temperature of the liquid and the chemical properties of the substances involved. This principle is often utilized in recrystallization processes to purify chemicals. A substance is dissolved in a hot solvent until it reaches saturation, and as the solvent cools, its solubility decreases, causing the excess solute to precipitate. Impurities, which are present in much smaller amounts, do not saturate the solvent and remain dissolved. If the conditions change, such as through cooling, and the concentration exceeds the saturation point, the solution becomes supersaturated. In the context of surface processes in physical chemistry, saturation describes the extent to which a binding site is fully occupied. For instance, base saturation refers to the proportion of exchangeable cations that are base cations. Similarly, in environmental soil science, nitrogen saturation occurs when an ecosystem, such as soil, can no longer store additional nitrogen. In organic chemistry, a saturated compound is one that contains no double or triple bonds. For example, in saturated linear hydrocarbons, each carbon atom is bonded to two hydrogen atoms, except for the terminal carbons, which are bonded to three hydrogen atoms. Methane, a simple saturated hydrocarbon, has a central carbon atom bonded to four hydrogen atoms. Alkanes are examples of saturated hydrocarbons, while alkenes are unsaturated. The degree of unsaturation indicates how much hydrogen a compound can bind. This concept also applies to the fatty acid components of lipids. Fats are classified as saturated or unsaturated based on whether their fatty acids contain carbon-carbon double bonds. Unsaturated fats have at least one double bond, and many vegetable oils contain fatty acids with one (monounsaturated) or multiple (polyunsaturated) double bonds. In organometallic chemistry, an unsaturated complex is one that has fewer than 18 valence electrons, making it prone to oxidative addition or the coordination of an additional ligand. Unsaturation is a common feature of many catalysts, as it is often necessary for the activation of substrates. In biochemistry, saturation refers to the proportion of total protein binding sites that are occupied at a given time.
